title: Facebook users' engagement with dental caries misinformation in Brazilian Portuguese
screen_reason: Content analysis of 500 Brazilian-Portuguese Facebook posts about dental caries, in which two calibrated coders judged each post's facticity against clinical guidelines and systematic reviews. Reports a share of items classified as misinformation (39.6%, 198/500) with an explicit denominator - a CONTENT estimate. The falsity judgement is made against an external ground truth (current scientific evidence on caries management), not a quality/usefulness score, so it is CONTENT rather than QUALITY.

estimates.country: Brazil (90.2% of posts; posts from 12 other, unnamed countries also present)
estimates.platform: Facebook (public pages and groups, via CrowdTangle)
estimates.date: posts published August 2016 to August 2021; dataset downloaded 26 August 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of dental caries-related Brazilian-Portuguese Facebook posts classified as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 198/500 (39.6%) [Table 3 column header 'Misinformation n = 198'; Table 1 facticity row 'Misinformation ... 198 (39.6%)']
estimates.denominator: 500 dental caries-related Facebook posts in Brazilian Portuguese, selected from the 88,134 posts retrieved by CrowdTangle keyword search and ranked by total user interaction (783 top-ranked posts screened; 36 off-topic, 225 duplicates and 22 dead links removed)
estimates.definition: a post presenting obvious false or misleading information about dental caries, judged against current scientific evidence from guidelines, consensuses and systematic reviews on the management of dental caries, that could potentially harm Facebook users
estimates.misinfo_def: "this study considered misinformation to be a broad term encompassing false or misleading content, regardless of whether or not there was intent to deceive or cause harm"
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was present in 39.6% of the posts, particularly those with a positive sentiment and commercial motivation.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; Results and Table 1 (Facticity row: Information 302 (60.4%), Misinformation 198 (39.6%)); Table 3 header 'Misinformation n = 198'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent, calibrated investigators (M.R. and O.S.J.) coded each post's facticity against current scientific evidence from guidelines, consensuses and systematic reviews on caries management; trained with a third investigator, calibrated on 10% of the sample (50 posts) until intra-examiner agreement >0.8; inter-examiner Intraclass Correlation Coefficient 0.80 to 0.98 across the coded variables; divergent posts re-accessed until consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: The search strategy ("carie" OR "carie" OR "caries" OR "lesoes cariosas" OR "dente cariado") was developed through exploratory analyses of hashtags and terms to ensure comprehensive coverage of dental caries-related content on Facebook. A dataset of 88,134 posts was downloaded in a .csv file format on August 26, 2021, covering a specific language (Portuguese) and timeframe (August 2016 to August 2021), with posts ranked by users' total interaction.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the 500 analysed posts are the top of an engagement ranking of 88,134 retrieved posts, not a random draw - the estimate is the misinformation share of the MOST-ENGAGED caries posts, which will not equal the share among all caries posts. Country coded Brazil (90.2% of posts) although 9.8% came from 12 other, unnamed countries; the sampling unit is the Brazilian-Portuguese language, not the country. year=2021 is the download/collection year; the posts themselves span Aug 2016 - Aug 2021. population_scope coded general_public because the corpus is open public posts, but note 94.2% came from business/dental-office/news-agency profiles rather than ordinary users.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted as separate rows: the subgroup misinformation shares in Tables 2-3, which are cross-tabs rather than the paper's headline - misinformation by sentiment (negative/neutral 51/173 = 29.5% vs positive 147/327 = 45.0%) and by motivation (noncommercial 166/444 = 37.4% vs commercial 32/56 = 57.1%), plus non-significant splits by total interaction, overperforming score, time of publication, author's profile and aim of content. Per the rule to keep the main figure rather than subgroup rows, only the overall 39.6% is extracted; the sentiment and motivation splits are the paper's analytic finding but are reported as odds ratios (OR 1.778 and 1.846) in the headline. NOT extracted: the non-misinformation descriptive shares (90.2% of posts from Brazil, 94.2% business profiles, 67.2% preventive, 88.8% noncommercial, 65.4% positive sentiment) - these characterise the corpus, not misinformation prevalence. NOT extracted: '36.5% of health misinformation' from a previous systematic review, and 'misinformation spreads 70% more than true news' (Grinberg et al.) - both figures the paper cites from elsewhere. The complement 302/500 (60.4%) accurate information is the same estimate inverted, not a second row.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of public Facebook posts. Frame: CrowdTangle keyword search in Portuguese ('carie' OR 'carie' OR 'caries' OR 'lesoes cariosas' OR 'dente cariado'), Aug 2016 - Aug 2021, downloaded 26 Aug 2021, yielding 88,134 posts ranked by total user interaction; the 783 highest-ranked were read in full and 500 retained after removing 36 off-topic, 225 duplicate and 22 link-unavailable posts (flowchart, Figure 1). No response rate (observational platform data); sample is engagement-ranked, not random, so it is not representative of all caries posts. Coding: two independent, calibrated investigators classified author's profile, sentiment, aim, motivation and facticity; calibration on 50 posts to intra-examiner agreement >0.8; inter-examiner ICC 0.80-0.98; disagreements resolved by consensus with a third investigator available. Analysis: Mann-Whitney U, chi-square, multiple logistic regression (alpha 0.05). Raw data anonymised and deposited in an open repository.
rob.item6_quote: A post was considered to contain misinformation only if it presented obvious false or misleading information that could potentially harm Facebook users.
rob.item10_quote: Misinformation was present in 39.6% of the posts, particularly those with a positive sentiment and commercial motivation.
